cells.tense: You are passing something on right now, and the passing carries your handwriting on it.
cells.ask: Show one person how you do the thing you are best at, and let them do it wrong once before you correct them.
cells.core:
You are the one handing it on. Quiet in the room, but the one who decides what is worth keeping and keeps it alive by using it rather than guarding it. Something older comes through you and comes out changed, and that change is part of why it lasts.

The adjusting is what makes it work: you watch what lands in the person across from you and you change the telling to fit them. That isn't watering it down. It is how a thing stays true across a gap of years. Keep doing that — the habit is already in your hands, and it is doing more than you give it credit for.
cells.sheetLine: You decide what's worth keeping, and you keep it alive.
cells.place: inside what people share and keep

cells.tense: You are defending something that was handed down as though the next person were a threat to it.
cells.ask: Pick one rule you've been holding firm and test whether it still does what it was meant to do.
cells.core:
You are holding the line past the point it needed holding. Ahead sits a picture of the doing coming out right, and you are living in that picture — so a conversation turns into a correction, and each correction makes the next one feel more necessary. The rules stopped carrying something and became the thing itself.

The windows are shut. The telling has gone stiff, and it costs you the people it was meant for. Keeping this means holding the rules loosely enough that whoever uses them can change them. Ask what the rule was for, and whether it still gets you there.
cells.sheetLine: You've been defending it instead of passing it on.
cells.place: inside what people share and keep

cells.tense: You came up without a shared way of doing things, and the blank page is still where a decision starts.
cells.ask: Wash the dishes, walk the same route, or cook one meal the same way twice this week, and notice what the repetition settles.
cells.core:
You build it alone, from nothing. No recipe handed down, no room where the way things are done here was ever shown to you — so a decision starts at the blank page, and knowing a lot doesn't help because none of it connects to anything older. It works. It is also tiring, and quiet in a way that is hard to say out loud.

Absent here is not more ideas. It is the plain shape underneath them — how a thing is done, passed on, and done again. Start with something small you can repeat on purpose. What gets built that way will hold people together, and you will not be holding it by yourself.
cells.sheetLine: You've been building from nothing. You don't have to.

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy, and you talk about it as though it were happening somewhere else.
cells.ask: Name one thing someone picked up from watching you and call it yours out loud, once.
cells.core:
People take things from you. The way you explain, what you shrug off, the thing you do without thinking — someone nearby has picked it up and is doing it now, and you would say it just happened. Going well, this is your way of doing something already out in the room and being used, and putting your name on it changes nothing about the thing itself.

The passing is real. The admitting isn't, and that is the whole gap. You don't have to claim a title or start teaching anybody. Look at one habit already traveling and say you are the one it came from, without adding anything to it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the one being copied. Say so plainly.
